extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating claims under 35 U.S.C. §101: identify whether a claim recites a judicial exception (abstract idea, law of nature, product of nature), explain the basis for that identification, and determine whether additional claim elements amount to 'significantly more' (Step 2B). Includes how to formulate rejections, evaluate applicant responses, and clarify the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify judicial exception as recited in the claim (products of nature)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a claim is alleged to recite a product of nature, the rejection should identify the exception as it is recited (i.e., set forth or described) in the claim, and explain using a reasoned rationale why the product does not have markedly different characteristics from its naturally occurring counterpart in its natural state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare the claimed subject matter to its closest naturally occurring counterpart and explain whether isolation produced a marked difference in structure, function, or other properties. See MPEP § 2106.04(b) for products of nature and § 2106.04(c) for the markedly different characteristics analysis. Sample explanation: recite X isolated from naturally occurring Y, compare X to X in its natural state; if no indication isolation resulted in marked difference, treat X as a product of nature exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain why additional claim elements do not amount to significantly more (Step 2B)
rubrics_metrics.description: After identifying the judicial exception, identify any additional elements recited in the claim beyond the exception and explain why they do not add significantly more to the exception. The explanation should address the additional elements both individually and as a combination when determining whether the claim as a whole recites eligible subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A rejection should be made only if it is readily apparent to an examiner relying on the examiner's expertise that the additional elements do not amount to significantly more. The examiner must provide a reasoned rationale so the applicant can respond. Conversely, when appropriate the examiner should explain why additional elements provide an inventive concept by adding a meaningful limitation. See MPEP § 2106.05 for considerations courts have found to qualify or not qualify as significantly more.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain why limitations are well-understood, routine, conventional
rubrics_metrics.description: When concluding particular claim limitations are well-understood, routine, conventional activities (or elements) to those in the relevant field, the rejection should explain why the courts have recognized, or those in the relevant field would recognize, those claim limitations as being well-understood, routine, conventional activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a reasoned explanation supporting that conclusion rather than just asserting conventionality. See MPEP § 2106.05(d) for more information and examples of elements that courts have found to be well-understood, routine, conventional activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic computer components/functions may not meaningfully limit the claim
rubrics_metrics.description: For claim limitations that recite a generic computer component performing generic computer functions at a high level of generality, examiners can explain why these generic computing functions do not meaningfully limit the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MPEP § 2106.05(f) lists computer functions courts have recognized as well-understood, routine, conventional when claimed in a merely generic manner. However, this is not universal: courts have found combinations of generic components can perform non-generic functions and thus amount to significantly more (e.g., DDR Holdings). Examiners should not assume all computer-implemented claims are ineligible and should analyze whether generic components in combination perform functions that are not merely generic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insignificant extra-solution activity and field-of-use limitations do not add meaningful limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim limitations that add insignificant extra-solution activity (e.g., mere data gathering, storing data) or that generally link use of the judicial exception to a particular technological environment or field of use do not meaningfully limit the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: adding a final step of storing data to a process that only recites computing a mathematical relationship does not add a meaningful limitation. Limiting use of an abstract idea to a particular industry (as in Flook) can be insufficient. See MPEP § 2106.05(g) for insignificant extra-solution activity and § 2106.05(h) for field-of-use/technological environment considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best practice: consult the specification and suggest claim amendments
rubrics_metrics.description: In the event a rejection is made, it is a best practice for the examiner to consult the specification to determine if there are elements that could be added to the claim to make it eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If such elements exist, the examiner should identify them in the Office action and suggest them as ways to overcome the rejection. This can assist the applicant in amending claims to recite significantly more than the judicial exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary requirements for §101 rejections (no evidence required but may be used)
rubrics_metrics.description: The courts consider the determination of whether a claim is eligible to be a question of law, so the court does not require evidence that a claimed concept is a judicial exception and generally decides eligibility without resolving factual issues. Similarly, at Step 2B there is no requirement for evidence to support a finding that the claim does not recite significantly more (e.g., that additional limitations are well-understood, routine, conventional activities).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If available, evidence may be provided to support an assertion or to rebut applicant arguments (e.g., specification statements, manuals, patents, court decisions). Care should be taken to ensure that facts of any cited case law comport with the facts of the application. Examples of cases demonstrating no evidence requirement are cited (e.g., FairWarning, OIP Techs., Content Extraction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use prior precedent to identify judicial exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: When determining whether claimed subject matter is judicially-excepted, the Federal Circuit typically compares the claimed subject matter to subject matter identified as an exception in its prior precedent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should examine earlier cases in which a similar or parallel descriptive nature can be seen and consider what prior cases were about and how they were decided. See Amdocs and other cited cases for examples of using precedent to identify abstract ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate applicant's response and reanalyze amended claims (2106.07(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: After examiners identify and explain the reasons why a claim is directed to a judicial exception without significantly more, the burden shifts to the applicant to amend or present persuasive arguments/evidence. Examiners must carefully consider all applicant's arguments and evidence rebutting the eligibility rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If applicant amends, determine the amended claim's broadest reasonable interpretation and perform the eligibility analysis again. If applicant's amendments/arguments persuasively establish eligibility, the rejection should be withdrawn. Applicant may argue that additional elements amount to significantly more individually or in combination (e.g., by improving technology, improving computer functioning, adding specific limitations other than conventional activity, or adding unconventional steps that confine the claim).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate examiner responses when maintaining a rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: If an applicant properly challenges the examiner's findings but the examiner deems it appropriate to maintain the rejection, the examiner must provide a rebuttal in the next Office action. Examples of appropriate rebuttals include explaining why the abstract idea is similar to that in the cited case, reevaluating conventionality claims and providing evidence where appropriate, assessing 'specially programmed' or 'particular machine' assertions, and reconsidering Steps 2A/2B with respect to improvements and preemption concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific examples: (1) explain why the abstract idea recited corresponds to an abstract idea in a cited Supreme Court or Federal Circuit decision; (2) if applicant disputes conventionality with argument/evidence, reevaluate and consider providing evidence to support the rejection; (3) mere addition of a generic computer/specially programmed computer does not automatically overcome eligibility rejections (Alice); (4) if applicant argues specificity or lack of preemption, reconsider whether claim improves computer functioning or technology and whether additional elements in combination amount to an inventive concept. See MPEP § 706.07(a) regarding new grounds of rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarify the record when claims are found eligible or to explain rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: When claims are deemed patent eligible, the examiner may make clarifying remarks on the record (e.g., reference the portion of the specification that describes the claimed improvement and note the claim elements that produce that improvement). Clarifying remarks may also be useful in explaining the rationale for a rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarifying remarks may be made at any point during prosecution and with a notice of allowance. Explaining the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) of a claim (for example, that a computer readable medium claim's BRI covers a carrier wave) will assist applicant in understanding and responding to a rejection and may include suggestions to overcome the rejection by submitting narrowing amendments.
